question: Why could the man who made the oldest known recording of a human voice never hear it?
answer: His machine only drew sound. Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville's phonautograph traced vibrations as wavy lines on soot-blackened paper, to be read by eye. His 1860 tracing of a voice singing Au clair de la lune was first played back in 2008, when researchers scanned the lines and converted them to sound.
move: An old record may hold more than its makers could read.
reference: Rosen, Researchers Play Tune Recorded Before Edison, The New York Times, 27 March 2008
